advances: Proves the complete registered two-resource scalar reflection bound with the absolute constant \(e^{-270}\). The proof selects an unbuffered center through the ordinary two-multiplier dual, rounds at most two fractional tied coordinates, and then creates both variance margins by shrinking at most \(6\sqrt n+2\) coordinates. This avoids assuming the simultaneous buffered-multiplier selection statement. Accepted fact `280b299bc1e87c14` then supplies the stated actual convex-body depth corollary for comparable exponential profiles on this two-resource support. The theorem does not assert the locked conjecture for general convex bodies.
author: research-agent
external_sources: None. The proof uses the one-dimensional maximizing-coordinate estimates from accepted fact `a3507c471fff4ad1` and the actual-fiber cutoff depth conclusion from accepted fact `280b299bc1e87c14`. The dual minimizer, feasible tied-coordinate average, rounding, simultaneous variance margins, and scalar mass comparison are proved above.
proof:
The set \(A\) is finite because its coordinates satisfy \(0\le z_i\le R/b_i\), and it contains zero. Thus \(\widetilde W>0\). If \(R=0\) or \(T=0\), strict positivity of the corresponding resource coefficients gives \(A=\{0\}\), so \(\widetilde S_0=\widetilde W=1\) and the scalar assertion holds. For its remaining proof, assume \(R,T>0\).

We use the following elementary one-dimensional conclusions proved in accepted fact `a3507c471fff4ad1`. For \(s>0\), the sequence \((2m+1)e^{-sm}\), over integers \(m\ge0\), attains its maximum. Its maximizing set consists of one integer or two consecutive integers. If \(m,m+1\) both maximize, then \(s=\log((2m+3)/(2m+1))\le\log3\). Every maximizing integer \(m\) satisfies

\[
2(1-e^{-s})(2m+1)e^{-sm}\ge\frac43,
\qquad sm\le2.
\tag{1}
\]

The second inequality also includes \(m=0\). These are the one-coordinate estimates in that accepted proof, before its single-resource center construction. We do not reuse that center construction for the present two-resource problem.

First we obtain an integer center with both resource inequalities and bounded dual slack, without variance margins. For \(s>0\), define \(f(s):=\max_{m\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}}\{\log(2m+1)-sm\}\), and put \(f(0):=+\infty\). On the nonnegative quadrant consider

\[
F(\lambda,\mu):=
\lambda R+\mu T+
\sum_{i=1}^n f(a_i+\lambda b_i+\mu c_i).
\tag{2}
\]

This is a convex extended-real function. For positive \(s\), the function \(f\) is locally a maximum of finitely many affine functions: in a neighborhood with \(s\ge\eta>0\), only finitely many integers can satisfy \(\log(2m+1)-sm\ge0\). Every maximizing integer does satisfy this inequality because the choice \(m=0\) has value zero. Thus \(f\) is continuous where finite. Also \(f(s)\to+\infty\) as \(s\downarrow0\): given any integer \(N\), its defining maximum is at least \(\log(2N+1)-sN\), whose limit is \(\log(2N+1)\), and these lower bounds are unbounded as \(N\to\infty\).

The value \(F(1,0)\) is finite because all \(b_i>0\). Since \(f\ge0\), one has \(F(\lambda,\mu)\ge\lambda R+\mu T\). Consequently every finite sublevel of \(F\) is bounded. A minimizing sequence in such a sublevel has a convergent subsequence in the closed quadrant. No argument \(a_i+\lambda b_i+\mu c_i\) can tend to zero along this subsequence, by the preceding divergence of \(f\). Continuity on the resulting positive arguments shows that the limit is a minimizer with finite value. Fix such a minimizer \((\lambda,\mu)\), and write \(s_i:=a_i+\lambda b_i+\mu c_i>0\) and \(q_i:=e^{-s_i}\).

Let \(\mathcal M_i\) be the maximizing integer set for the \(i\)-th coordinate at \(s_i\), and let \(B:=\prod_i\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal M_i)\). Each interval in this box is a singleton or has consecutive integer endpoints. There exists \(x\in B\) with

\[
b\cdot x\le R,\qquad c\cdot x\le T,
\qquad
\lambda(R-b\cdot x)=\mu(T-c\cdot x)=0.
\tag{3}
\]

Here is an elementary justification that covers a minimizer on either boundary of the multiplier quadrant. Let \(G:=\{(R-b\cdot x,T-c\cdot x):x\in B\}\), a compact convex subset of \(\mathbb R^2\). Let \(Q\) be the closed cone of vectors whose first coordinate is zero when \(\lambda>0\) and nonnegative when \(\lambda=0\), and whose second coordinate is zero when \(\mu>0\) and nonnegative when \(\mu=0\). The desired assertion is precisely \(G\cap Q\ne\varnothing\).

Suppose instead these sets were disjoint, and take a pair \(g_0\in G\), \(u_0\in Q\) minimizing their distance. Such a pair exists, and the distance is positive, because \(G\) is compact and \(Q\) is closed. Set \(v:=u_0-g_0\ne0\). Minimizing along segments in the two convex sets gives \(v\cdot g\le v\cdot g_0\) for every \(g\in G\), and \(v\cdot u\ge v\cdot u_0\) for every \(u\in Q\). Since \(Q\) is a cone, the latter inequality with \(u=0,2u_0\) gives \(v\cdot u_0=0\). Thus \(\max_{g\in G}v\cdot g\le-\|v\|^2<0\). Also \(v_1\ge0\) if \(\lambda=0\), and \(v_2\ge0\) if \(\mu=0\), by taking the corresponding coordinate unit vector in \(Q\).

It follows that \(v\) is a feasible direction from \((\lambda,\mu)\) into the quadrant for sufficiently small positive steps. Locally, (2) is a maximum of finitely many affine functions, and its active affine functions are indexed by \(m\in\prod_i\mathcal M_i\). Their directional slopes along \(v\) are \(v\cdot(R-b\cdot m,T-c\cdot m)\), all strictly negative by the preceding bound. Since the collection is finite, a sufficiently small positive step decreases all active functions and keeps each inactive function below the old value. It therefore decreases \(F\), contradicting minimality. This proves (3).

Consider now the nonempty compact polytope of vectors \(x\in B\) satisfying the two resource inequalities in (3), with the first imposed as an equality if \(\lambda>0\) and the second imposed as an equality if \(\mu>0\). Choose an extreme point \(x\) of this polytope. At most two of its coordinates are nonintegral. Indeed, if three or more were strictly inside their consecutive-integer intervals, there would be a nonzero vector supported on three such coordinates and orthogonal to both \(b\) and \(c\). Sufficiently small perturbations in both directions along that vector would remain in all intervals and preserve both resource sums, contradicting extremality.

Put \(m_i:=\lfloor x_i\rfloor\). Each \(m_i\) belongs to \(\mathcal M_i\), and positivity of \(b,c\) gives \(b\cdot m\le R\) and \(c\cdot m\le T\). Complementarity in (3) yields

\[
\begin{aligned}
D&:=\lambda(R-b\cdot m)+\mu(T-c\cdot m)\\
&=\sum_i(\lambda b_i+\mu c_i)(x_i-m_i)
\le2\log3.
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}
\]

To see the last bound, only the at most two nonintegral coordinates contribute. For each, both \(m_i,m_i+1\) maximize, so \(s_i\le\log3\); also \(0<x_i-m_i<1\) and \(0\le\lambda b_i+\mu c_i\le s_i\). Thus (4) includes all boundary and tie cases.

Next we create the two variance margins by changing few coordinates of \(m\). For any \(z\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^n\) and any real coefficient vector \(r\), write \(\sigma_r(z)^2:=\sum_i r_i^2z_i(z_i+1)/3\). Let \(k:=\min\{n,\lceil3\sqrt n\rceil\}\). Choose a set \(I_b\) of \(k\) indices on which \(b_im_i\) are largest, and independently choose a set \(I_c\) of \(k\) indices on which \(c_im_i\) are largest. Resolve any ties arbitrarily, and let \(I:=I_b\cup I_c\). Define the final integer center by \(j_i:=\lfloor m_i/4\rfloor\) for \(i\in I\) and \(j_i:=m_i\) for \(i\notin I\). Then \(|I|\le2k\le6\sqrt n+2\), and

\[
b\cdot j+2\sigma_b(j)\le b\cdot m\le R,
\qquad
c\cdot j+2\sigma_c(j)\le c\cdot m\le T.
\tag{5}
\]

To prove these two statements at once, fix \(r\in\{b,c\}\), let \(I_r\) be its selected set, and put \(U:=\sum_{i\in I_r}r_im_i\). The resource reserved by shrinking these coordinates satisfies \(r\cdot(m-j)\ge3U/4\). Also \(j_i\le m_i/4\) on \(I_r\), so \(\sum_{i\in I_r}(r_ij_i)^2\le U^2/16\). If \(k<n\), every \(r_im_i\) outside \(I_r\) is at most \(U/k\), and hence \(\sum_{i\notin I_r}(r_ij_i)^2\le nU^2/k^2\le U^2/9\). If \(k=n\), that outside sum is zero, so the same bound holds. Shrinking any additional coordinates selected for the other resource can only improve these inequalities. For every nonnegative integer \(j_i\), one has \(j_i(j_i+1)\le2j_i^2\). Therefore

\[
\sigma_r(j)^2
\le\frac23\sum_i(r_ij_i)^2
\le\frac23\left(\frac1{16}+\frac19\right)U^2
=\frac{25}{216}U^2.
\]

Since \(25/54<9/16\), this implies \(2\sigma_r(j)\le3U/4\le r\cdot(m-j)\). The assertion is also valid when \(U=0\). This proves (5).

The change of center has a controlled cost in box cardinality:

\[
\prod_i(2j_i+1)\ge7^{-|I|}\prod_i(2m_i+1).
\tag{6}
\]

For each changed coordinate, write \(m_i=4t+s\) with integers \(t\ge0\) and \(0\le s\le3\). Then \(j_i=t\), and \(2m_i+1=8t+2s+1\le7(2t+1)=7(2j_i+1)\). Unchanged coordinates contribute no loss. Notice also that \(a\cdot j\le a\cdot m\), because \(a_i\ge0\).

Since \(m_i\) is maximizing, (1) gives \(a_im_i\le s_im_i\le2\). When \(m_i\ge1\), it follows that \(a_i^2m_i(m_i+1)/3\le4(m_i+1)/(3m_i)\le8/3\); when \(m_i=0\), the term is zero. Since \(j\le m\) coordinatewise, we obtain

\[
\sigma_a(j)^2\le\sigma_a(m)^2\le\frac{8n}{3}.
\tag{7}
\]

Let \(V_i\) be independent and uniform on \(\{-j_i,\ldots,j_i\}\). The scalar products \(a\cdot V,b\cdot V,c\cdot V\) have mean zero and variances \(\sigma_a(j)^2,\sigma_b(j)^2,\sigma_c(j)^2\). Chebyshev's inequality and a union bound give

\[
\mathbb P\bigl\{
|a\cdot V|\le2\sigma_a(j),\quad
|b\cdot V|\le2\sigma_b(j),\quad
|c\cdot V|\le2\sigma_c(j)
\bigr\}\ge\frac14.
\tag{8}
\]

A zero-variance scalar product is identically zero and contributes no exceptional event. On the event in (8), the two endpoints \(j\pm V\) are nonnegative integer vectors, and (5) puts both in \(A\). Their minimum weight is \(e^{-a\cdot j-|a\cdot V|}\). Uniformity on the box, followed by (6), (7), and \(a\cdot j\le a\cdot m\), therefore gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
\widetilde S_j
&\ge\frac14e^{-a\cdot j-2\sigma_a(j)}\prod_i(2j_i+1)\\
&\ge\frac14\,7^{-|I|}
e^{-a\cdot m-2\sqrt{8n/3}}\prod_i(2m_i+1).
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}
\]

For \(z\in A\), the nonnegative multipliers give \(e^{-a\cdot z}\le e^{\lambda R+\mu T}\prod_iq_i^{z_i}\). Extending the sum to the full nonnegative orthant yields \(\widetilde W\le e^{\lambda R+\mu T}\prod_i(1-q_i)^{-1}\). Combining this bound with (9), then using (1), (4), and the bound on \(|I|\), gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\widetilde S_j}{2^{-n}\widetilde W}
&\ge\frac14\,7^{-|I|}e^{-2\sqrt{8n/3}-D}
\prod_i\bigl[2(1-q_i)(2m_i+1)q_i^{m_i}\bigr]\\
&\ge\frac14\exp\left(
n\log\frac43-2\sqrt{\frac{8n}{3}}-2\log3
-(6\sqrt n+2)\log7\right).
\end{aligned}
\tag{10}
\]

There is no new dual-slack term for the shrunk center in this comparison: (9) compares its weight directly to \(e^{-a\cdot m}\), and the dual estimate is still evaluated at the unbuffered maximizing center \(m\).

Finally, \(\log(4/3)\ge1/4\), \(2\sqrt{8/3}\le4\), and \(\log7,\log3,\log4<2\). The logarithm of the last expression in (10) is consequently at least

\[
\frac n4-16\sqrt n-10
=\left(\frac{\sqrt n}{2}-16\right)^2-266
\ge-266>-270.
\]

This proves the claimed scalar bound for all \(R,T\ge0\).

For the actual-body corollary, retain the objects \(C_z,w_z,W,S,h_S\) from the statement, with their meanings in accepted fact `280b299bc1e87c14`. Apply the scalar conclusion to choose \(j\in A\). For each displacement put \(\alpha(v):=\min\{w_{j+v},w_{j-v}\}\), and let \(\mathcal U_j:=\{v:\alpha(v)>0\}\), exactly as in that accepted fact. The support and comparison hypotheses imply \(\alpha(v)\ge(K/M)\min\{\widetilde w_{j+v},\widetilde w_{j-v}\}\) for every integer \(v\), and \(W\le KM\widetilde W\). Hence

\[
\sum_v\alpha(v)
\ge\frac K M\widetilde S_j
\ge\frac{Ke^{-270}}M\,2^{-n}\widetilde W
\ge\frac{e^{-270}}{M^2}\,2^{-n}W.
\tag{11}
\]

For \(v\in\mathcal U_j\), define \(\Delta_j(v):=\log(w_j^2/(w_{j+v}w_{j-v}))\), using precisely the accepted curvature. It is nonnegative by `280b299bc1e87c14`. Both endpoints are in \(A\), and the profile comparison gives

\[
\frac{w_j^2}{w_{j+v}w_{j-v}}
\le
\frac{(KM e^{-a\cdot j})^2}
{(KM^{-1}e^{-a\cdot(j+v)})(KM^{-1}e^{-a\cdot(j-v)})}
=M^4.
\]

Thus \(0\le\Delta_j(v)\le4\log M\), so the accepted cutoff sum \(B_j^\Delta(4\log M)\) equals \(\sum_v\alpha(v)\). The actual body has \(W>0\), since \(w_0\ge K/M>0\), and \(w_j>0\). The cutoff conclusion of `280b299bc1e87c14`, evaluated at this center and cutoff, therefore supplies one point \(p^\star\in S\) with

\[
h_S(p^\star)
\ge\frac{\ell}{16}
\frac{B_j^\Delta(4\log M)}{1+4\log M}
\ge\frac{\ell e^{-270}}{16M^2(1+4\log M)}\,2^{-n}W,
\]

where the last step is (11). The point is selected before the ambient halfspace, as required by that accepted conclusion. The scale \(K\) cancels, and the bound is independent of the continuous dimension. This establishes the stated corollary under its explicit support and profile hypotheses.
statement:
Let \(n\ge1\) be an integer, let \(a_i\ge0\) and \(b_i,c_i>0\) for \(1\le i\le n\), and let \(R,T\ge0\). Put \(A:=\{z\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^n:b\cdot z\le R,\ c\cdot z\le T\}\). Define \(\widetilde w_z:=e^{-a\cdot z}\) for \(z\in A\) and \(\widetilde w_z:=0\) for \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus A\), and put \(\widetilde W:=\sum_z\widetilde w_z\) and \(\widetilde S_j:=\sum_{v\in\mathbb Z^n}\min\{\widetilde w_{j+v},\widetilde w_{j-v}\}\). The displacement sum is oriented and includes zero. Then there exists \(j\in A\) such that \(\widetilde S_j\ge e^{-270}2^{-n}\widetilde W\). This extends the support class in accepted fact `a3507c471fff4ad1`; the tilded quantities have the same scalar-profile meaning as in that fact.

For the actual-body consequence, let \(d\ge1\), let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^d\) be a convex body, put \(C_z:=\{x:(z,x)\in C\}\), and let \(w_z:=\operatorname{vol}_d(C_z)\). Suppose its positive-volume integer-fiber support is exactly \(A\), and suppose there are \(K>0\), \(M\ge1\) such that \(KM^{-1}e^{-a\cdot z}\le w_z\le KM e^{-a\cdot z}\) for every \(z\in A\). Put \(W:=\sum_{z\in\mathbb Z^n}w_z\), \(S:=C\cap(\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^d)\), and let \(h_S(p)\) be the infimum of \(\mathcal H_d(S\cap H)\) over all closed ambient halfspaces containing \(p\). These untilded objects have exactly their meanings in accepted fact `280b299bc1e87c14`. With \(\ell:=-\log(1-e^{-1})\), there exists one point \(p^\star\in S\) satisfying

\[
h_S(p^\star)\ge
\frac{\ell e^{-270}}{16M^2(1+4\log M)}\,2^{-n}W.
\]

For each fixed \(M\), this positive constant is independent of \(n,d,a,b,c,R,T,K\). All logarithms are natural.
